newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Greece to aid Albania, legalise immigrants' status.
newsitem.headline: Greece to aid Albania, legalise immigrants' status.

text.p: Greece agreed on Tuesday to legalise the status of thousands of illegal Albanian immigrants in return for help in fighting cross-border crime, and pledged millions of dollars in aid to reconstruct the Balkan state.

In the first visit to Tirana by a foreign government minister since elections last month, Greek Foreign Minister Theodoros Pangalos said Athens would help Albania rebuild its economy, armed forces and police.
"Greece is interested in the existence of a strong, democratic Albania and we are determined to contribute to this end," Pangalos told a news conference at the end of a one-day visit.

Pangalos said a group of Greek military experts supported by a unit of 100 soldiers would remain in Albania to help reform the army after most of a 7,000-strong multinational protection force leaves the country by mid-August.

The world community has been eager to help Albania return to stability after months of unrest. International donors are due to meet in Brussels in October to examine ways to provide aid in the form of approved projects.
More than 1,500 people have been killed in Albania since March, when violence broke out following the collapse of bogus pyramid investment schemes.

The turmoil led to the fall of the Democratic Party government and the resignation of president Sali Berisha. The Socialist Party and its allies won a landslide victory in an early general election held last month.
Pangalos said Greece would also help Albania strengthen ties with the European Union to secure EU aid for projects worth millions of dollars.
Greece itself has pledged some two billion drachmas ($7 million) of direct aid and a further 18 billion drachmas ($60 million) for development projects.

In a protocol signed by Pangalos and Albanian Foreign Minister Paskal Milo, the two countries agreed that temporary work permits would be issued to Albanians, who are now often summarily expelled from Greece.
Thousands of Albanian families, many of them left destitute after the pyramid scheme scam came to light, rely on remittances sent from relatives abroad.
"Mr Pangalos promised that Albanian immigrants in Greece will be treated equally with other immigrants. This is good news for Albania," Milo told reporters.

Relations between the neighbours worsened drastically in 1994 when Greece expelled thousands of Albanian immigrants after Albanian ethnic Greek leaders were put on trial for spying. Ties were restored a year later.

The influx of illegal Albanian immigrants into Greece, estimated at around 300,000, has taxed the Greek economy and police forces have struggled to hold back a wave of crime washing across Greece's northern border.
"Greece is interested in protecting its border not only because of illegal immigrants but mainly over the smuggling of drugs (and) weapons," Greek Interior Minister George Romeos said.
